paper_metadata.title: QuantumLeap: Hybrid quantum neural network for financial predictions

summary: The paper proposes QuantumLeap, a hybrid deep quantum neural network for predicting stock prices using sliding windows of 4 trading days across 24 securities (407 training days, 20‑day forecast horizon). The model was trained as a classical simulation on an HP Apollo cluster (≈24 h total runtime) and reports lower RMSV than classical baselines—for example AAPL RMSV 2.83 vs 6.05 (classical NN) and 8.37 (ARIMA)—with most daily prediction errors below 1% and maxima around 8%.

experiments.description: Hybrid deep quantum neural network (QuantumLeap) for financial time-series prediction on 24 stocks, evaluated in regression and 20-day extrapolation regimes, compared against a classical neural network and ARIMA baseline.

algorithm.variant: deep quantum neural network / hybrid quantum neural network (QuantumLeap)
algorithm.ansatz: layered unitary operators / quantum perceptron network
algorithm.optimizer: Adam for classical measurement network; quantum unitary updates via gradient-based update rule in Eq. (8)/(13)

problem_formulation.encoding_details: each sliding window of 4 trading days is mapped to a complex state vector and density matrix using low/high prices; one quantum network per stride predicts a later density matrix
problem_formulation.objective_function: maximize fidelity between predicted output density matrix and target output density matrix
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: state-vector normalization via Eq. (18); minimum prices treated as hidden parameters/constraints

problem_instance.description: Predict stock high prices from low/high time-series windows for 24 securities over a 20-trading-day forecast horizon

dataset_specification.train_test_split: first 407 trading days for training, last 20 trading days for testing

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: financial time series partitioned with sliding window of size 4; low/high values encoded into complex state vectors; output is maximum price reached during the day
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: regression on training regime and extrapolation on last 20 days; relative error reported per day; RMSV comparison against classical NN and ARIMA; Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test on error distributions

implementation_details.classical_solver: Adam-trained classical neural network and ARIMA baseline
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: sliding-window partitioning; low/high price encoding; normalization of state vectors
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: classical dense network measures maximum price from predicted density matrix
implementation_details.total_execution_time: approximately 24 h for all 24 stocks (training 24 × 20 = 480 hybrid networks in parallel batches)

speedup_claims.caveats: The paper claims computational tractability and parallelisation across strides, but does not provide a quantified asymptotic or empirical speedup over classical methods.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: computationally tractable in terms of number of hidden layers; layer-by-layer training reduces memory requirements

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: not specified; algorithm implemented only as classical simulation of a quantum neural network using matrix operators (32×32 and 128×128 unitaries)
limiting_factors: No qubit counts or circuit depths reported
Model implemented via classical matrix simulation on HPC
No complexity analysis or asymptotic speedup
Performance comparison is against classical ML baselines but using a simulated quantum model

notes: The paper describes a quantum neural network built from unitary operators and density matrices, but does not report an actual gate-based hardware platform, qubit count, circuit depth, or gate counts. The unitary dimensions (e.g., 32x32, 128x128) are matrix sizes, not explicit qubit counts, so num_qubits remains null. The paper compares against a classical neural network and ARIMA, which are baselines, not separate quantum experiments.

Authors claim their quantum approach outperforms a classical neural network and ARIMA in RMSV (Table 5), but the 'quantum' model is simulated on classical HPC and no gate‑level quantum implementation or complexity advantage is demonstrated.
